prompt: Which chemist discovered the nucleophilic substitution reaction by interconverting the pure (+)- and (−)-malic acids?

choices.why: Fischer praised the discovery as the most remarkable observation in optical activity since Pasteur, but the work was Walden's.
Hughes and Ingold proposed the S_N2 mechanism in 1937, decades after the discovery itself.
Fischer compared the discovery to Pasteur's fundamental observations, but Pasteur didn't make it.

explanation: Discovery of the nucleophilic substitution reaction of alkyl halides dates back to the German chemist Paul Walden, who found that the pure enantiomeric (+)- and (−)-malic acids could be interconverted through a series of simple substitution reactions.

prompt: In what year was the work carried out that first revealed nucleophilic substitution, the interconversion of the (+)- and (−)-malic acids?
explanation: Paul Walden's work on interconverting (+)- and (−)-malic acids dates to 1896. Further studies in the 1920s and 1930s clarified how the inversions of configuration occur.

prompt: In Walden's cycle, what did he isolate when he treated (−)-malic acid with PCl5?

choices.why: (−)-Chlorosuccinic acid came from (+)-malic acid. (−)-Malic acid gave the (+) acid.
(+)-Malic acid formed only in the next step, when the chlorosuccinic acid was treated with wet Ag2O.
Walden isolated an optically active product, (+)-chlorosuccinic acid, not a racemic mixture.

explanation: In Walden's cycle, (−)-malic acid + PCl5 gave (+)-chlorosuccinic acid, which gave (+)-malic acid on treatment with wet Ag2O. Similarly, (+)-malic acid gave (−)-chlorosuccinic acid and then (−)-malic acid.

prompt: In Walden's cycle, which reagent converted (+)-chlorosuccinic acid into (+)-malic acid?

choices.why: PCl5 did the opposite job: it converted malic acid into chlorosuccinic acid.
Acetate ion was the nucleophile in the later 1-phenyl-2-propanol cycle, not in Walden's malic acid cycle.
That reagent forms tosylates, used in the 1920s–1930s studies of 1-phenyl-2-propanol.

explanation: Treating (+)-chlorosuccinic acid with wet Ag2O gave (+)-malic acid, and treating (−)-chlorosuccinic acid the same way gave (−)-malic acid. PCl5 was used for the malic acid → chlorosuccinic acid steps.

prompt: Why did Walden's results show that some step in his cycle must have occurred with inversion of configuration at the chirality center?

choices.text: (−)-Malic acid was converted into its enantiomer, (+)-malic acid
The sign of rotation changed from (−) to (+) when malic acid became chlorosuccinic acid
choices.why: The sign of rotation isn't directly related to configuration, so one sign change proves nothing. The proof is that the cycle turned one enantiomer into the other.

choices.text: Both chlorosuccinic acids he isolated were racemic
choices.why: He isolated optically active (+)- and (−)-chlorosuccinic acids, not racemic mixtures.

choices.text: PCl5 and wet Ag2O each racemized the malic acid
choices.why: A racemizing step would give optically inactive material, but Walden obtained optically active (+)-malic acid.

explanation: Because (−)-malic acid was converted into (+)-malic acid, its enantiomer, some reactions in the cycle must have occurred with a change, or inversion, of configuration at the chirality center. The cycle alone didn't reveal which steps, or how.

prompt: Can you tell from the sign of optical rotation alone whether a reaction changed the configuration at a chirality center?

choices.text: No, because the direction of light rotation and the configuration of a chirality center aren't directly related
Yes, because a change from (+) to (−) always means inversion has occurred
choices.why: Sign and configuration aren't directly related, so a change of sign doesn't by itself prove inversion.

choices.text: Yes, because a product with the same sign as the reactant always has the same configuration
choices.why: For the same reason, keeping the sign doesn't prove that the configuration is unchanged.

choices.text: Only for compounds containing a halogen, whose rotation follows their configuration
choices.why: There is no such exception. For any compound, the sign of rotation doesn't reveal the configuration.

explanation: As Section 5.5 showed, the direction of light rotation and the configuration of a chirality center aren't directly related. You can't tell by looking at the sign of rotation whether a change in configuration has occurred during a reaction.

prompt: What do chemists today call the kind of transformation that takes place in each step of Walden's cycle?

choices.why: No double bond forms. In each step one nucleophile takes the place of another.
Nothing adds across a multiple bond. In each step one group substitutes for another.
The groups exchanged are nucleophiles (Cl− and HO−), not radicals, so these are nucleophilic substitutions.

explanation: The transformations in Walden's cycle are nucleophilic substitution reactions, because each step involves the substitution of one nucleophile (chloride ion, Cl−, or hydroxide ion, HO−) by another. They are among the most common and versatile reaction types in organic chemistry.

prompt: Which two nucleophiles take each other's place in the steps of Walden's cycle?

choices.why: No bromine is involved. PCl5 introduces chlorine, giving chlorosuccinic acid.
Those two take part in the later 1-phenyl-2-propanol cycle, not in Walden's malic acid cycle.
Cyanide appears in the section's worked example, not in Walden's cycle.

explanation: Each step in Walden's cycle substitutes one nucleophile, chloride ion (Cl−) or hydroxide ion (HO−), by the other: malic acid's –OH is replaced by –Cl to give chlorosuccinic acid, and the –Cl is replaced by –OH to regenerate malic acid.

prompt: In nucleophilic substitution reactions, how does the section suggest you think about an alkyl para-toluenesulfonate (tosylate) group?

choices.text: As if it were simply a halogen substituent
As the nucleophile that attacks the alkyl carbon
choices.why: The tosylate is the group that gets replaced, so it plays the part of the halide, not the nucleophile.

choices.text: As a group that can never be displaced
choices.why: Tosylate is displaced by acetate ion in step 2 of the 1-phenyl-2-propanol cycle.

choices.text: As a group that is always replaced with retention of configuration
choices.why: Substitution of tosylate by acetate is exactly the step where the configuration is inverted.

explanation: For all practical purposes, the entire tosylate group acts as if it were simply a halogen substituent. When you see a tosylate in a molecule, do a mental substitution and tell yourself you're dealing with an alkyl halide.

prompt: In the cycle that interconverts the enantiomers of 1-phenyl-2-propanol, step 1 turns the alcohol into its tosylate. Why does this step leave the configuration at the chirality center unchanged?

choices.text: It breaks the O–H bond of the alcohol, not the C–O bond to the chiral carbon
It breaks the C–O bond, but the tosylate bonds back on the same side
choices.why: The C–O bond to the chirality center isn't broken at all during tosylate formation.

choices.text: The chirality center is destroyed and then re-formed with the same configuration
choices.why: No bond to the chiral carbon is broken, so the center is never destroyed.

choices.text: It inverts the configuration, but step 3 inverts it back again
choices.why: Step 1 doesn't touch the chiral carbon, and step 3 doesn't break the C–O bond at the chirality center either.

explanation: Formation of the tosylate occurs by breaking the O–H bond of the alcohol rather than the C–O bond to the chiral carbon, so the configuration around that carbon is unchanged.

prompt: In the three-step cycle that interconverts (+)- and (−)-1-phenyl-2-propanol, which step inverts the configuration at the chirality center?

choices.text: Step 2, nucleophilic substitution of tosylate ion by acetate ion
Step 1, formation of the tosylate from the alcohol
choices.why: Step 1 breaks the O–H bond, not the C–O bond to the chiral carbon, so the configuration is unchanged.

choices.text: Step 3, cleavage of the acetate ester by hydroxide ion
choices.why: Step 3 takes place without breaking the C–O bond at the chirality center.

choices.text: All three steps, each inverting the chirality center in turn
choices.why: Steps 1 and 3 don't break a bond to the chirality center, so they can't change its configuration.

explanation: Since (+)-1-phenyl-2-propanol is converted into its (−) enantiomer, at least one step must invert the chirality center. Steps 1 and 3 don't break a bond to that carbon, so the inversion must take place in step 2, where acetate ion substitutes for tosylate ion.

prompt: In the three-step cycle that interconverts the enantiomers of 1-phenyl-2-propanol (tosylate formation, substitution by acetate, cleavage of the acetate by hydroxide), in how many of the steps is a bond to the chirality center broken?
explanation: Only step 2, the nucleophilic substitution of tosylate by acetate, breaks a bond to the chiral carbon. Step 1 breaks the O–H bond, and step 3 cleaves the acetate without breaking the C–O bond at the chirality center.

prompt: From the 1-phenyl-2-propanol cycle and nearly a dozen similar series, what did researchers conclude about nucleophilic substitution?

choices.text: Substitution of a primary or secondary alkyl halide or tosylate always proceeds with inversion of configuration
Substitution of any alkyl halide or tosylate, including a tertiary one, always proceeds with inversion
choices.why: Tertiary alkyl halides and tosylates give different stereochemical results and react by a different mechanism.

choices.text: Substitution of a primary or secondary alkyl halide always proceeds with retention of configuration
choices.why: The cycles showed that the substitution step inverts the configuration.

choices.text: Substitution of a primary or secondary alkyl halide or tosylate always gives a racemic product
choices.why: The products were optically active with inverted configuration, not racemic.

explanation: Researchers concluded that the nucleophilic substitution reaction of a primary or secondary alkyl halide or tosylate always proceeds with inversion of configuration. Tertiary alkyl halides and tosylates react by a different mechanism and give different stereochemical results.

prompt: Assuming inversion of configuration, what product forms when (R)-1-bromo-1-phenylethane undergoes nucleophilic substitution with cyanide ion, CN−?

choices.why: That would mean retention. With inversion, and –CN taking bromine's place as the top-priority group, R becomes S.
The question assumes inversion, which gives a single enantiomer, not a racemic mixture.
That is just the enantiomer of the reactant. The substitution replaces –Br with –CN.

explanation: Replace –Br with –CN and invert the chirality center (Worked Example 11.1.1). In the reactant the priorities are –Br > –C6H5 > –CH3 > –H; in the product they are –CN > –C6H5 > –CH3 > –H (the nitrile carbon carries N,N,N, which beats the ring carbon's C,C,C). The new top group sits opposite where Br was, so R becomes (S)-2-phenylpropanenitrile.

prompt: Assuming inversion of configuration, what product forms when (S)-2-bromohexane undergoes nucleophilic substitution with acetate ion, CH3CO2−?

choices.why: That keeps the original configuration. With inversion, and the acetate oxygen taking bromine's place as the top priority, S becomes R.
Acetate replaces bromine on carbon 2, the carbon that held it, not on carbon 1.
Substitution of a secondary bromide is assumed to occur with inversion, which gives a single enantiomer.

explanation: Acetate replaces bromine at carbon 2 with inversion (Exercise 11.1.1). The priorities keep the same pattern (–Br or –O2CCH3 > butyl > –CH3 > –H), so inverting the center turns S into R: (R)-1-methylpentyl acetate, CH3CO2CH(CH3)CH2CH2CH2CH3.
